items.title: J&K Advocate General's post vacant since October 2024; PIL in High Court seeks appointment
items.summary: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court has issued a notice to the J&K government on a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition seeking immediate appointment of an Advocate General for the Union Territory [Harsh Dubey V/s UT of J&K] A Division Bench of Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajnesh Oswal directed the Chief Secretary and Law Secretary to respond to the PIL by October 21, the next date of hearing. The Court observed that the post of Advocate General should ideally be filled by the next date. Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajnesh Oswal Advocate General's post in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir has remained vacant since the resignation of Advocate General DC Raina in October 2024. Raina resigned after the Omar Abdullah-led National Conference government took charge in the Union Territory. Since then, the Lieutenant Governor and National Conference government haven't been able to fill the vital post. The PIL filed by advocate Harsh Dubey has sought directions to the competent authority to take immediate steps to fill the constitutional post. As per the petition, the continued vacancy of the constitutional office is affecting the administration of justice and the discharge of statutory functions attached to the post. The plea points out that the vacancy has also impacted the functioning of the Jammu and Kashmir Advocates Welfare Fund Trustee Committee since the Advocate General serves as its ex-officio Chairperson under the Advocates’ Welfare Fund Act, 2001. When will Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh get an Advocate General? High Court asks The petition was filed through advocate Kannu Karan Prasher.

items.title: PIL before Bombay High Court challenges State rule on abortions beyond 24 weeks
items.summary: The Bombay High Court has issued notice to Maharashtra government on a public interest litigation (PIL) petition challenging the instructions that require women to seek court order for the medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) beyond 24 weeks [Dr Rajeev Joshi v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] A division bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna sought the State's response and scheduled the matter for hearing on October 9. Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna The petition filed by the Medico Legal Society of India (MLSI) through pediatrician Dr. Rajeev Joshi challenges a June 2024 Maharashtra Government Resolution (GR). Under the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy is permitted up to 24 weeks subject to prescribed conditions, while terminations beyond 24 weeks are highly restricted. The June 2024 GR mandates direct court intervention for all other late-term cases. MLSI has argued that this requirement imposes financial and emotional burdens on victims by forcing them into prolonged litigation. The plea contends that the government is improperly shifting its administrative and clinical responsibilities to the judiciary. The PIL also highlighted severe clinical and ethical dilemmas associated with late-term abortions. Medical terminations performed beyond 24 weeks frequently result in live premature births, creating an urgent need for specialised neonatal intensive care. However, India faces a critical shortage of Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) beds to manage such fragile infants. As per the plea, the legal risks and severe distress faced by medical professionals. The plea refers to an FIR registered against a gynaecologist in Satara for performing a court-ordered abortion. According to the petition, doctors are currently caught between conflicting judicial mandates, ethical duties, and the threat of criminal prosecution. Hence, the petition has sought quashing the court intervention clause in the 2024 GR for late-term abortions. It has also sought a clear standard operating procedure (SOP) for late-term pregnancies. Further, the State should bear the financial costs of intensive neonatal care for any child born alive during court-authorized procedures, the plea states. Joshi appeared in person. Government pleaders Neha S Bhide, OA Chandurkar and MM Pabale appeared for State. [Read order]

items.title: Kerala HC grants relief to woman denied use of frozen embryos by IVF hospital after her husband's death
items.summary: The Kerala High Court recently came to the aid of a 43-year-old widow who was denied the use of embryos she had preserved along with her husband during his lifetime at a hospital for assisted reproduction or In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF). The hospital, which had refused to give the widow the frozen embryos, claimed that there was no clear indication of whether her husband wanted them to be handed over to his wife following his death. The consent form signed by the couple only envisaged three scenarios about the fate of the embryos if either spouse were to die: (i) that the embryos be used by an unknown couple (ii) that the embryos be used for research or (iii) that the embryos be destroyed. Left with only these three options, the husband had opted for the use of the embryos by an unknown couple. Justice Harishankar V Menon noted that no option was given for the handover of the embryos to the wife. The judge also pointed out such a consent form deviated from the prescribed format in which consent was supposed to be taken from couples undergoing IVF. Under the relevant rules, an option has to be provided for the handover of the embryos to the surviving spouse if either spouse were to die. The Court concluded that husband, in this case, clearly intended for the embryos to be put to use rather than destroyed. It added that the wife's interest in becoming a parent must be respected, and her wish cannot be rejected merely because the hospital failed to obtain the husband's consent properly. " It is specifically found that it is the 'deceased’s inferred consent' and the 'partner’s interest' in becoming a parent that require the utmost consideration. As has been found, the intention of the deceased was to ensure the ‘actual use’ of the embryos, and, therefore, the wish of the petitioner-wife to become a parent deserves to be respected, " the Court held. Justice Harishankar V Menon Therefore, the Court ordered the hospital to handover the frozen embryos to the widow. The September 1 ruling was passed on a plea by a woman who had undergone infertility treatment along with her husband at a hospital in Thiruvananthapuram. Their embryos were cryopreserved during the husband's lifetime. After the husband's death, the wife sought to use the preserved embryos for IVF treatment. items.summary: Using a vernacular version of a registered trademark may still amount to infringement if it is phonetically and visually similar to the original mark, the Madras High Court has held [Vikas Vs Shanghai Huanqiu]. Justice K Kumaresh Babu made the observation while restraining Vikas Mandoth from using the Tamil version of the “GLOBE” trademark on padlocks. “ The defendants attempt to use a phonetically and visually similar trademark/ device however, in a vernacular language would not entitle him to infringe the trademark of the plaintiff which had been established to have a good reputation and good will, ” the Court said in an order passed on September 7. Justice K Kumaresh Babu The suit was filed by Shanghai Huanqiu Lock Making Company Limited and Valaram, the proprietor of Prince Impex (plaintiffs). The plaintiffs said Shanghai Huanqiu manufactures locks under the GLOBE trademark and had built substantial reputation and goodwill in India and other countries. They alleged that Mandoth was selling padlocks bearing the word “Globe” in Tamil. According to them, the Tamil mark was phonetically and visually similar to their mark and was likely to confuse customers. They also alleged that Mandoth had copied the artistic work, colour combination, trade dress and overall appearance of their padlocks. On November 28, 2025, the High Court passed an ex parte injunction restraining Mandoth from using the disputed mark. He then filed applications seeking to vacate the injunction. Mandoth argued that his Tamil mark had been developed independently after considering the nature and function of the product. He added that the mark was registered and, therefore, he could not be prevented from using it. He also claimed that he was a prior user of the Tamil mark. However, the Court noted that Mandoth’s trademark application, filed in 2023, stated that the mark was “proposed to be used”. items.title: Can gifts to lover become loans after break-up? Singapore High Court answers
items.summary: The Singapore High Court on September 9 rejected a claim by TCI Express CEO and Managing Director Chander Agarwal seeking S$468,090 from his former girlfriend, holding that money spent on her during their relationship could not later be treated as loans. [Chander Agarwal Vs Lee Xiu] Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin found that the evidence overwhelmingly showed that Agarwal intended the disputed sums to be gifts to Felicia Lee, with whom he was in a relationship from September 2022 to around December 2023. Agarwal and Lee first met on a flight in 2019 and later began meeting after he contacted her on Facebook. They entered into a romantic relationship in September 2022, which continued until around December 2023. During and even before the relationship, Agarwal spent substantial sums on Lee, including on luxury goods, travel, credit-card expenses, insurance premiums, feng shui services and an executive programme. After suspecting Lee of infidelity, Agarwal ended the relationship and sued her in March 2024. He claimed that various sums totalling S$468,090 were not gifts but interest-free loans which Lee had agreed to repay. The disputed amounts included spending on AMEX and Citibank cards, first-class trips to the US and Hong Kong, life insurance, a fashion company, feng shui services and programme fees. Lee denied the claim, maintaining that the expenses were gifts made out of love and affection. Explaining why the claim failed, the Court said: “ The evidence before me points overwhelmingly to the Claimant having intended the Disputed Sums as gifts to the Defendant. The theme running through the Claimant’s case is his theory that once the Defendant accepted his offers to pay, these moneys automatically became loans.” The Court said that a valid gift is made where there is an intention to gift and delivery of the subject matter. Crucially, it is the donor’s intention at the time the money is transferred that determines its character. items.title: Madras HC quashes animal cruelty case against man accused of pelting stone at dog that bit him
items.summary: The Madras High Court recently quashed an animal cruelty case registered against a man accused of pelting a stone at his neighbour’s pet dog, after the dog allegedly bit and injured him [ Balaji v. State ]. Justice GK Ilanthiraiyan found that the police had investigated the non-cognisable offence without obtaining the necessary prior permission from the jurisdictional magistrate, as required under Section 174(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). Justice GK Ilanthiraiyan The Court was dealing with a plea filed by one, Balaji, to quash an animal cruelty case filed against him for allegedly pelting a stone at his neighbour's pet dog. Balaji and the dog’s owner, Devaraj Manikkam, were neighbours with a history of disputes. Balaji alleged that Manikkam would maliciously set his dog upon him whenever he walked along the street. The dog eventually bit Balaji’s leg and caused serious injuries, prompting him to lodge a police complaint. The Peerkankaranai police registered a case against Manikkam under Section 291 (negligent conduct with respect to an animal in one's possession) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Manikkam subsequently complained that Balaji had pelted a stone at his dog. Based on this complaint, the police registered another First Information Report (FIR) and charged Balaji under Section 11(1)(a) of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. Balaji approached the High Court to quash the case. He argued that the animal cruelty proceedings were merely a counterblast to his earlier complaint against Manikkam. The Court noted that no evidence had been produced to show that the dog suffered any injury because of the alleged stone pelting. Balaji, on the other hand, submitted medical records and photographs supporting his allegation that the dog had bitten him. The Court further noted that an offence under Section 11(1)(a) of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act was non-cognisable. Therefore, the police could not register an FIR and investigate the allegation without first obtaining permission from the jurisdictional court. items.title: I was arrested due to political reasons; it was complainant who attacked me: Swatantra Bhardwaj to Delhi court
items.summary: Right-wing influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj, accused of assault, told a Delhi court on Monday that he was arrested by the Delhi Police due to political reasons and that it was the complainant who attacked him and not the other way around. Bhardwaj is accused of assaulting of the father of a student-activist during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protests at Jantar Mantar in July. He is currently in jail in connection with the same. However, his counsel Umesh Sharma told the Court today that there is a video of the complainant attacking him, but the Delhi Police has taken no action against the complainant. "Police ko wo video nazar nahi aa raha... Is video m clearly dikhai de raha hai ki complainant is mujhpe attack kiya hai aur main gir gaya hu (The police are not able to see that video. It is clearly visible in this video that the complainant attacked me and I fell down),” Sharma told Additional Sessions Judge (ASJ) Saurabh Pratap Singh Laler. The Court was hearing Bhardwaj's bail application in-camera. Sharma told the Court that Bhardwaj was arrested in the FIR under the provisions of the SC/ST Act, another FIR under POCSO was registered against him. "The police issued me a notice on June 27 to appear for questioning, and I appeared for questioning on June 29. After that, I was allowed to go. Then, after some political developments, I was arrested on September 4. After my arrest, a new FIR [under POCSO] was registered," Sharma said. On the other hand, advocate Swati Khanna appeared for the complainant and stated that Bhardwaj used casteist slurs against the complainant and even admitted on a video that it was he who attacked the complainant. Khanna also informed the Court that Bhardwaj had filed a habeas corpus plea in the Delhi High Court and the same has been rejected. Meanwhile, Delhi Police told the Court that when the complaint was first registered, no mention was made of a casteist slur, later when the statement was recorded again, a casteist slur was mentioned, and therefore the SC/ST Act, was invoked. After hearing the arguments, the Court reserved its verdict. Bhardwaj was arrested from Uttar Pradesh on September 5 for allegedly assaulting the father of a Dalit student-activist during the CJP protests at Jantar Mantar in July. He has been booked for offence of assault and provisions under the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act [SC/ST Act] and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act). items.title: Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, Khaitan & Co, A&O Shearman act on Pernia's Pop Up Shop ₹680 crore IPO
items.summary: Pernia’s Pop Up Shop (Purple Style Labs Limited) has raised ₹680 crore from an initial public offering of equity shares. Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas advised Pernia's Pop Up Shop on this IPO. The transaction was led by Manan Lahoty (Partner, Head - Capital Markets) and Priyadarshini Rao (Partner), with support from Radhika Pandey (Principal Associate), Associate Anomitra Debnath, Khushi Parekh and Nikshetaa Jain. Manan Lahoty, Priyadarshini Rao Khaitan & Co acted as the legal counsel to the book running lead managers Axis Capital Limited and IIFL Capital Services Limited on this IPO. The transaction team consisted of Subhayu Sen (Partner), Aparna Bagree (Partner), Ira Pandya (Senior Associate), Aayush Virani (Senior Associate), Associats Ria Chaudhary and Aayushi Poddar (Associate). Subhayu Sen, Aparna Bagree A&O Shearman acted as international counsel for the BRLMs. The transaction was led by Pallavi Gopinath Aney (Partner), along with Serena Upadhyay (Senior Associate). Pallavi Gopinath Aney Pernia’s Pop Up Shop is a vibrant and carefully curated design platform promoted by Abhishek Agarwal. Based in Mumbai, India, the platform offers a diverse range of products, including bridal trousseau selections, festive attire, ethnic wear, ready-to-wear collections, and designer menswear. items.title: Hyderabad’s groundwater risky for kids, shows high nitrate and fluoride levels: Study
items.summary: Groundwater in several parts of Hyderabad has elevated levels of nitrate and fluoride, with children facing higher potential non-carcinogenic health risks, according to a recent study. The study analysed 44 groundwater samples collected during the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon seasons of 2023. According to a TNIE report , nitrate exceeded the permissible drinking-water limit of 45 mg/L in 36% of the samples collected before monsoon and 40% of the samples collected after monsoon. Nitrate concentrations ranged from 3 to 230 mg/L during the pre-monsoon period and from 5 to 797 mg/L post-monsoon, with higher levels mainly recorded in southwestern and central parts of the city. Researchers attributed nitrate contamination largely to fertiliser use, sewage infiltration, septic-tank leakage and urban wastewater. Monsoon rainfall can also carry nitrogen compounds from the soil into groundwater, the study noted. Fluoride exceeded the acceptable limit of 1 mg/L in 64% of pre-monsoon samples and 59% of post-monsoon samples. Concentrations ranged from 0.21 to 3.03 mg/L before the monsoon and 0.28 to 5.94 mg/L afterwards, with higher levels found in northern, southern and southwestern areas. Unlike nitrate, fluoride enrichment was attributed mainly to the weathering of granitic rocks and prolonged interaction between groundwater and aquifer materials. The study's health-risk assessment found that the hazard quotient (HQ) for nitrate and fluoride exceeded 1 at several locations. The mean HQ for fluoride among children increased from 1.04 before the monsoon to 1.11 afterwards. For nitrate, it increased from 1.81 to 3.78. The combined total hazard index (THI) for children increased from 3.07 to 3.78, compared with an increase from 2.27 to 2.79 among adults. Under US Environmental Protection Agency guidelines, an HQ above 1 indicates a potential non-carcinogenic health risk. The study considered children more vulnerable because of their lower body weight and greater exposure relative to body mass. The groundwater samples also showed elevated total dissolved solids (TDS) in 95% of pre-monsoon samples and 86% of post-monsoon samples, against the Bureau of Indian Standards' permissible limit of 500 mg/L. Total hardness exceeded the permissible limit in 75% of samples collected before the monsoon and 84% of those collected afterwards. The study was conducted by Achiraju Pallavi and Allam Edukondal of Osmania University, Laxman Kumar Duvva of JNTU-Hyderabad and Ratnakar Dhakate

items.title: Ways to Rebuild Credit Using a Credit Card
items.summary: You apply for a personal loan only to find that your application is rejected or offered at a higher interest rate because of a low credit score. This can happen when you have missed payments in the past, used too much of your available credit or have not borrowed enough to build a credit history. However, with consistent and responsible use, you can make a Credit Card a useful tool for rebuilding your credit profile over time. It will prove that you can borrow and repay what you owe. 6 Ways to Rebuild Credit Using a Credit Card Start With a Card You Can Manage If your credit history is limited or your score is low, apply for a Credit Card whose eligibility requirements and credit limit match your financial situation. For example, you can apply for a secured Credit Card backed by a fixed deposit. Since the card is backed by collateral, it may be easier to access it than unsecured cards. Pay Your Credit Card Bill on Time Your payment history is one of the most important parts of your credit profile. Repaying your dues on time shows that you can responsibly manage borrowed money. Late or missed payments, on the other hand, can negatively affect your credit score. You can set up reminders or enable automatic payments so that you do not miss the due date. More importantly, try to pay the total amount due in full rather than carrying forward a balance. Keep Your Credit Utilisation Low Credit utilisation is the amount of your available credit that you are currently using. For example, if your Credit Card limit is ₹1 lakh and your outstanding balance is ₹30,000, your utilisation is 30%. High utilisation can make you appear more dependent on borrowed money and may negatively affect your credit profile. Credit bureaus recommends keeping utilisation low rather than regularly using a large portion of your available limit. This does not mean you should spend unnecessarily just to show activity. Use the card for planned expenses that you can repay. Pay More Than the Minimum Due The minimum amount due is not the same as clearing your Credit Card bill. Paying only the minimum can leave a balance outstanding. This can result in interest charges and will keep your utilisation higher. Whenever possible, pay the total amount due by the payment deadline. This helps you avoid revolving debt while maintaining a consistent repayment record. items.title: BJP protests Ganesha procession curbs in T Narsipur, police say there are none
items.summary: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Sunday, September 13, protested in Karnataka’s T Narsipur over alleged curbs on a Ganesha procession, even as the district police said there was no restriction on the route or the festival. The protest was held after T Narsipur Police Inspector Dhananjaya warned Ganesha procession organisers against bursting crackers in front of a mosque on Link Road, reports said. The BJP interpreted the remarks as restrictions on the procession and demanded the inspector’s suspension. Leader of Opposition R Ashoka, Mysuru-Kodagu MP Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, MLA TS Srivatsa, former MP Pratap Simha and other BJP leaders joined the protest. Ashoka carried a Ganesha idol and led a march along the Link Road. The BJP leaders were later detained by the police and subsequently released. However, Mysuru Superintendent of Police Mallikarjuna Baladandi said there was no restriction on Ganesha processions in T Narsipur and that organisers could follow the traditional routes used in previous years. The town has around 15 to 20 Ganesha pandals every year, with processions held on different days, he said. SP Mallikarjuna said the inspector’s remarks were made during a peace meeting held on September 7. Organisers had been asked to inform the police about the dates of immersion and the routes of their processions so that adequate security arrangements could be made. The SP said a Ganesha group had taken out a procession last year without informing the police. Since the police were not aware of the procession, security arrangements could not be made, even though the procession passed by a mosque. The inspector’s warning was therefore meant to ensure that organisers did not take out processions without informing the police, SP Mallikarjuna said. SP Mallikarjuna also said the inspector had not prohibited processions from passing along Link Road or imposed a ban on celebrations near the mosque. He said the traditional routes remained open this year. He further said the inspector’s statement had been presented in a “different” manner on social media, leading to confusion. Police officials have since been instructed against making statements that could create confusion among the public. items.title: BRICS explained: The bloc’s origins, members and its challenge to the global order
items.summary: The flags of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and other countries were lined up in New Delhi this weekend as leaders gathered for the 18th BRICS Summit. Hosted by India on September 12 and 13, the summit came at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions, wars in West Asia and Ukraine, US tariffs and growing debates over who gets to shape the global economic and political order. The group adopted a 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration, covering issues ranging from global trade and sanctions to artificial intelligence, critical minerals, health, climate change and reform of international institutions. The declaration also called for restraint in West Asia, criticised unilateral tariffs and sanctions, and backed reforms to the global financial and trading systems without naming the countries involved. But what exactly is BRICS? Why was it formed? And is it really a challenge to the US-led global order? What is BRICS? BRICS is a grouping of major emerging economies that cooperate on political, economic and development issues. The acronym BRIC was coined by Goldman Sachs in 2001 to describe Brazil, Russia, India and China as major emerging economies with the potential to become some of the world's largest economies. The four countries began formalising their cooperation in 2006, and held their first summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. South Africa joined in 2011, turning BRIC into BRICS. The group expanded again in 2024, when Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates became full members. Indonesia joined as a full member in January 2025. BRICS currently has 11 members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Indonesia. BRICS does not function like the European Union or NATO. It has no founding treaty, permanent secretariat or common budget. The presidency rotates among members, and the grouping operates primarily through consultations among leaders, ministers and officials, along with cooperation in areas such as trade, finance, health, technology, agriculture, energy and development. The grouping presents itself as a platform for the Global South, broadly referring to developing and emerging countries seeking a greater voice in global affairs. The 2026 New Delhi Declaration said BRICS would continue to amplify the concerns and priorities of the Global South and called for a more representative and multipolar international system. items.title: Hyderabad: 26-year-old woman killed after TGSRTC bus hits bike taxi
items.summary: A 26-year-old woman named Hema Vajjiparthi was killed after a state transport bus allegedly crashed into a two-wheeler. Hema had hailed a bike taxi ride from Banjara Hills and was passing through Srinagar Colony when the accident happened on September 12, Saturday. Panjagutta police booked the driver, Sheik Anwar, and reportedly arrested him on the same day. He was booked under sections 106(1) (causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide) and 125(a) (act endangering life of others) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and section 184 (driving dangerously) of the Motor Vehicles Act. According to the police complaint lodged by the bike taxi driver Hemachala Patro (48), who drives for ride-hailing apps such as Uber and Rapido, he received a booking from Hema around 3 pm on September 12 to pick her up from BNR Colony, Venkat Nagar, Banjara Hills. Hema was a native of East Godavari district in Andhra Pradesh and was working as a customer relationship executive at a car showroom in Banjara Hills, according to reports . Hemachala said he picked up Hema on his red-coloured Glamour bike and was going towards the drop location through Srinagar Colony. Around 3.30 pm, when they were near My Home Madhuban Apartments, an electric bus allegedly approached from behind at a very high speed and hit his bike from the rear. Hemachala alleged that the driver, Sheik Anwar, was driving in a rash and negligent manner. Hemachala said that both he and Hema fell onto the road, and the bus ran over her head, killing her on the spot. Hemachala was shifted to Meditech Hospital in Panjagutta to treat his injuries. His complaint alleged that the accused was driving the bus at a very high speed and in a rash and negligent manner, thereby causing the death of Hema and injuring him.

items.title: Urvashi’s Aasha is refreshing because its women are allowed to be complicated
items.summary: Cinema has rarely allowed women the complexity of being human. Female characters are most often expected to be virtuous, predictable, and ideal. Even when women are placed at the centre of the narrative, few and far as they are, the contradictions are neatly ironed out into palatable ideas of femininity. Aasha , however, offers an interesting aside. Directed by Safar Sanal, the Malayalam film released on September 11. “I have never lived for myself,” says Urvashi’s titular character, in a moment of absolute frenzy. The film opens at a bank. Aasha waits patiently for her turn, though visibly restless. Soon enough, we meet the short-tempered, stubborn woman beneath the one who puts up with everything, one who is not reluctant to make a scene at the slightest hint of disrespect. As the narrative unfolds, we see her running around to oversee the construction of her elder daughter’s (Lakshmi Menon) new home and arrange a good alliance for the younger one. For a widow living alone with her young daughter in a big city, Aasha appears unbothered by social judgement on the outside. It is when she reaches for her nerve relaxants at night that we get to see her shaky hands and apprehensive eyes. But when Anagha refuses to back down from a romantic relationship with a man from a marginalised background, Aasha’s fury springs back. The density of Aasha’s anxious rage, however, spills over when she gets into a late-night accident involving a volatile man (Joju George). We see the darkness inside her, and the lengths to which she is capable of going to earn the respect she is owed.
